l: speakers (the lamenting community), The Lamentations of Jeremiah, Chapter 5
s: The speakers lament that their inheritance and houses have gone to strangers, that they are orphaned, must buy water and wood, are pursued, weary, and ruled by servants, and have given their hands to Egypt and Assyria for bread. They acknowledge that their fathers sinned and that they themselves have sinned, and they plead for the LORD to turn them and renew their days.

l: Zion, The Lamentations of Jeremiah, Chapter 5
s: Zion's women were ravished, and its mountain is described as desolate, with foxes walking on it. The speakers' hearts are faint and their eyes dim because of it.

l: sin and iniquity, The Lamentations of Jeremiah, Chapter 5
s: The speakers say their fathers sinned and are no more, and that they bear their fathers' iniquities. They also confess, 'Woe to us, for we have sinned!', linking the fallen crown and their suffering to sin.

l: desolation and suffering of Jerusalem, The Lamentations of Jeremiah, Chapter 5
s: The text lists the suffering: loss of inheritance, orphanhood, paid-for water and wood, pursuit, famine, sword danger, skin blackened like an oven, and rule by servants. Women in Zion and the cities of Judah were ravished, princes were hanged by their hands, young men carried millstones, children stumbled under wood, and the elders' gate-seat and the young men's music ceased. Joy turned to mourning, and Zion's mountain lies desolate.

l: The Book of Ezekiel, The Book of Ezekiel, Chapter 1
s: Ezekiel the priest, son of Buzi, is among the captives by the river Chebar in the Chaldeans' land in the fifth year of King Jehoiachin's captivity when the heavens open and he sees visions of God. The LORD's word comes to him and the LORD's hand is on him. He sees a stormy wind and fiery cloud from the north, out of which come four living creatures, each with four faces and four wings, moving straight forward wherever the spirit goes. Beside them are wheels within wheels with rims full of eyes, moving with the creatures because the creature's spirit is in the wheels. Above an awesome crystal-like expanse is a sapphire throne with a man-like figure of glowing metal and fire surrounded by rainbow-like brightness, which Ezekiel identifies as the likeness of the LORD's glory, and he falls on his face and hears a voice speaking.

l: Ezekiel, The Book of Ezekiel, Chapter 1
s: Ezekiel is identified as the priest, son of Buzi, among the captives by the river Chebar in the land of the Chaldeans, in the fifth year of King Jehoiachin's captivity. The LORD's word comes to him and the LORD's hand is on him, and he sees visions of God. After seeing the likeness of the LORD's glory he falls on his face and hears a voice that speaks.

l: the LORD, The Book of Ezekiel, Chapter 1
s: The LORD's word comes to Ezekiel the priest, and the LORD's hand is on him by the river Chebar. The brightness around the man-like figure on the throne is described as the appearance of the likeness of the LORD's glory, like a rainbow in the cloud on a rainy day.

l: cherubim, The Book of Ezekiel, Chapter 1
s: Four living creatures with the likeness of a man come out of a fiery cloud; each has four faces (man, lion on the right, ox on the left, eagle) and four wings, straight feet like a calf's sparkling like burnished bronze, and human hands under the wings. They go straight forward without turning wherever the spirit goes, look like burning coals and torches with lightning, and run and return like flashes. Their wings sound like great waters and the voice of the Almighty, and they let their wings down when they stand.

l: wheels (beside the living creatures), The Book of Ezekiel, Chapter 1
s: A wheel on the earth stands beside each living creature, appearing like beryl, as a wheel within a wheel, moving in four directions without turning. Their high, dreadful rims are full of eyes all around. They go, stand and are lifted up together with the living creatures, because the spirit of the living creature is in the wheels.

l: sapphire throne (above the cherubim), The Book of Ezekiel, Chapter 1
s: Above the crystal-like expanse over the creatures' heads is the likeness of a throne, appearing like a sapphire stone. A likeness of a man is on it above.

l: man-like figure (on the throne), The Book of Ezekiel, Chapter 1
s: On the throne is a likeness with the appearance of a man. From the waist upward he looks like glowing metal with fire within, and from the waist downward like fire, with brightness around him like a rainbow in the cloud. Ezekiel says this was the likeness of the LORD's glory.

l: visions of God, The Book of Ezekiel, Chapter 1
s: The heavens are opened and Ezekiel sees visions of God, in the thirtieth year, fourth month, fifth day, among the captives by the river Chebar. The visions include the stormy wind and fiery cloud, the four living creatures, the wheels, the expanse, the throne and the man-like figure in brightness.

l: The Book of Ezekiel, The Book of Ezekiel, Chapter 2
s: In Chapter 2, a speaker addresses the "son of man" and tells him to stand, and the Spirit enters the narrator and sets him on his feet. The Lord GOD sends the son of man to the children of Israel, described as a rebellious, impudent, stiff-hearted nation whose fathers and who themselves have transgressed to this day. He is to speak the words "This is what the Lord GOD says," whether they hear or refuse, so that they will know a prophet has been among them. He is told not to fear them or their words, though he dwells among briers, thorns, and scorpions, and not to be rebellious himself but to open his mouth and eat what is given. A hand holds out a scroll, which is spread before him, written on both sides with lamentations, mourning, and woe.

l: Ezekiel, The Book of Ezekiel, Chapter 2
s: The son of man is told to stand, and the Spirit enters him and sets him on his feet so he hears the speaker. He is sent to the children of Israel to speak the words of the Lord GOD whether they listen or not, and is commanded not to fear them, not to be rebellious, and to open his mouth and eat what is given. He sees a hand holding a scroll, which is spread before him.

l: the LORD, The Book of Ezekiel, Chapter 2
s: The Lord GOD speaks to the son of man, sends him to the rebellious children of Israel, and instructs him to say 'This is what the Lord GOD says.' He commands the son of man not to fear and not to rebel, and he gives him something to eat, with a hand holding out a scroll written with lamentations, mourning, and woe. His purpose is that the people will know a prophet has been among them.

l: house of Israel, The Book of Ezekiel, Chapter 2
s: The children of Israel are called a nation of rebels who have rebelled against the speaker, as have their fathers, to this very day. They are described as impudent, stiff-hearted, and a rebellious house, and their words and looks are something the son of man must not fear. Whether they hear or refuse, they will know a prophet has been among them.

l: scroll (the scroll Ezekiel eats), The Book of Ezekiel, Chapter 2
s: A hand stretched out to the narrator holds a scroll of a book. It is spread before him and is written within and without, containing lamentations, mourning, and woe.

l: rebellion, The Book of Ezekiel, Chapter 2
s: Rebellion marks the children of Israel and their fathers, who have transgressed against the speaker to this very day, and the people are repeatedly called a rebellious house, even 'most rebellious.' The son of man is warned not to be rebellious like that house. Their rebellion does not prevent the prophet's message from being sent.

l: The Book of Ezekiel, The Book of Ezekiel, Chapter 3
s: In Chapter 3, the LORD commands Ezekiel, addressed as "son of man," to eat a scroll, which tastes as sweet as honey, and to speak the LORD's words to the house of Israel. The LORD warns that Israel will not listen because they are obstinate and hard-hearted, so he makes Ezekiel's face and forehead hard like a diamond. The Spirit lifts Ezekiel up and carries him in bitterness to the captives at Tel Aviv by the river Chebar, where he sits overwhelmed for seven days. The LORD then appoints Ezekiel a watchman, explaining that he will be held responsible for warning the wicked and the righteous. Finally, the LORD tells Ezekiel to shut himself in his house, where he will be bound and made mute until the LORD opens his mouth to speak.

l: Ezekiel, The Book of Ezekiel, Chapter 3
s: Ezekiel is told to eat the scroll, which he does, and is commanded to speak the LORD's words to the house of Israel. His forehead is made hard like a diamond, the Spirit carries him in bitterness to the captives at Tel Aviv by the river Chebar, and he sits overwhelmed for seven days. He is then made a watchman, told to shut himself in his house, and warned that he will be bound and made mute until the LORD opens his mouth.

l: the LORD, The Book of Ezekiel, Chapter 3
s: The LORD commands Ezekiel to eat the scroll and speak to the house of Israel, and makes his face and forehead hard against their opposition. He appoints Ezekiel a watchman and says he will require the blood of those Ezekiel fails to warn. His glory appears again in the plain, and he says he will make Ezekiel mute and open his mouth only when he chooses to speak.

l: house of Israel, The Book of Ezekiel, Chapter 3
s: The house of Israel is described as obstinate, hard-hearted and rebellious, and the LORD says they will not listen to Ezekiel because they will not listen to him. They are contrasted with peoples of strange speech who would have listened. Ezekiel is sent to them, particularly to the captives, to say "This is what the Lord GOD says," whether they hear or refuse.

l: scroll (the scroll Ezekiel eats), The Book of Ezekiel, Chapter 3
s: The LORD gives Ezekiel the scroll and has him eat it, filling his belly and bowels with it. It is as sweet as honey in his mouth, and eating it precedes his commission to speak the LORD's words to Israel.

l: watchman role, The Book of Ezekiel, Chapter 3
s: The LORD makes Ezekiel a watchman to the house of Israel, charged to hear the word from his mouth and warn them for him. If Ezekiel fails to warn, the LORD will require the blood of the one who dies at his hand. If he warns and the person does not turn, Ezekiel has delivered his own soul.

l: the wicked, The Book of Ezekiel, Chapter 3
s: When the LORD says a wicked person will surely die, the watchman must warn him to turn from his wicked way. If Ezekiel gives no warning, the wicked man dies in his iniquity and the LORD requires his blood from Ezekiel. If warned and he does not turn, he dies in his iniquity but Ezekiel is free of blame.

l: the righteous, The Book of Ezekiel, Chapter 3
s: If a righteous man turns from his righteousness and commits iniquity, and the LORD lays a stumbling block before him, he will die, and his former righteous deeds will not be remembered. If Ezekiel fails to warn him, the LORD will require his blood at Ezekiel's hand. If Ezekiel warns him and he does not sin, he will surely live and Ezekiel has delivered his soul.

l: The Book of Ezekiel, The Book of Ezekiel, Chapter 4
s: In Chapter 4, the LORD instructs a man addressed as 'son of man' to portray Jerusalem on a tile and enact a siege against it, with an iron pan as a wall between himself and the city, as a sign to the house of Israel. He is told to lie on his left side 390 days to bear the iniquity of the house of Israel, then on his right side 40 days to bear the iniquity of the house of Judah, bound with ropes and facing the siege with his arm uncovered. He must eat bread made of wheat, barley, beans, lentils, millet, and spelt by weight, and drink water by measure, baking it over dung in the people's sight. The speaker objects that he has never been polluted, so the LORD permits cow's dung instead of human dung. The LORD explains that this foreshadows Israel eating unclean bread among the nations and that He will break the staff of bread in Jerusalem, leaving the people dismayed and pining away in their iniquity.

l: Ezekiel, The Book of Ezekiel, Chapter 4
s: Addressed as 'son of man', he is commanded to portray Jerusalem on a tile, enact a siege, lie 390 days on his left side and 40 days on his right to bear the iniquity of Israel and Judah, and be bound with ropes. He is to eat rationed mixed-grain bread and drink measured water. When told to bake it over human dung, he protests that he has never eaten anything unclean, and the LORD allows cow's dung instead.

l: the LORD, The Book of Ezekiel, Chapter 4
s: The LORD commands the sign-acts of the tile, the iron pan, the lying on each side, and the rationed bread and water. He explains that Israel will eat unclean bread among the nations where He drives them. He relents on human dung in favor of cow's dung after the protest, and declares that He will break the staff of bread in Jerusalem.

l: Jerusalem, The Book of Ezekiel, Chapter 4
s: Jerusalem is portrayed on a tile and symbolically besieged with forts, a mound, camps, and battering rams. The LORD declares that He will break its staff of bread, so its people will eat bread by weight and drink water by measure in fearfulness and dismay.

l: house of Israel, The Book of Ezekiel, Chapter 4
s: The house of Israel is the audience of the sign, and its iniquity is borne by the man lying on his left side for 390 days, one day for each year of iniquity. The LORD says its children will eat their bread unclean among the nations where He will drive them.

l: siege of Jerusalem (tile depiction), The Book of Ezekiel, Chapter 4
s: The siege is enacted on a tile with forts, a mound, camps, and battering rams all around, and an iron pan serves as a wall of iron between the man and the city. He faces it with his arm uncovered and prophesies against it, and it serves as a sign to the house of Israel.

l: iniquity (of Israel and Judah), The Book of Ezekiel, Chapter 4
s: The iniquity of the house of Israel is to be borne for 390 days, a day for each appointed year, and that of the house of Judah for 40 days. In the end, the people lack bread and water, are dismayed with one another, and pine away in their iniquity.

l: bread (mixed-grain bread), The Book of Ezekiel, Chapter 4
s: The bread is made from wheat, barley, beans, lentils, millet, and spelt in one vessel, eaten for 390 days at twenty shekels by weight per day. It is baked as barley cakes in the people's sight over dung, changed from human to cow's dung after the protest. It symbolizes the unclean, rationed bread of Israel and the breaking of Jerusalem's staff of bread.

l: The Book of Ezekiel, The Book of Ezekiel, Chapter 5
s: The Lord GOD commands the prophet, addressed as 'son of man', to shave his head and beard with a sharp sword and divide the hair by weight into thirds: one burned in the city, one struck with the sword, and one scattered to the wind, with a few strands bound in his robe and some of those burned again. The Lord GOD explains that the hair represents Jerusalem, which He set in the middle of the nations but which rebelled against His ordinances and statutes more than the surrounding countries. Because Jerusalem defiled His sanctuary with detestable things, He declares He is against her, will execute unparalleled judgments before the nations, and will show no pity. A third of the people will die by pestilence and famine, a third will fall by the sword, and a third will be scattered with a sword drawn after them, including the horror of fathers and sons eating one another. Jerusalem will become a desolation, reproach, taunt and warning to the surrounding nations, as the Lord sends famine, evil animals, pestilence, blood and the sword until His wrath is accomplished.

l: the LORD, The Book of Ezekiel, Chapter 5
s: The Lord GOD instructs the prophet in the sign-act of the shaved hair and then interprets it as judgment on Jerusalem. He declares Himself against her, swears by His life that He will show no pity, and promises to execute judgments before the nations until His wrath is accomplished and He is comforted. He affirms that all this is spoken in His zeal and that people will know He is the LORD.

l: Ezekiel, The Book of Ezekiel, Chapter 5
s: The son of man is commanded to take a sharp sword like a barber's razor, shave his head and beard, weigh the hair on balances, and divide it into three parts. He is to burn one third, strike another around with the sword, scatter the last to the wind, and bind a few hairs in his robe, burning some of those too. His actions symbolically enact the fate of Jerusalem.

l: Jerusalem, The Book of Ezekiel, Chapter 5
s: Jerusalem is identified as the city the Lord set in the middle of the nations, yet she has rebelled against His ordinances and statutes more than the surrounding countries and defiled His sanctuary. She is told the Lord is against her and will bring unprecedented judgment: cannibalism in her midst, death by pestilence, famine and sword, and scattering of a remnant. She will become a desolation, reproach, taunt, instruction and astonishment to those around her.

l: nations, The Book of Ezekiel, Chapter 5
s: The nations surround Jerusalem, and the Lord says she has been more wicked and turbulent than they, though they themselves rejected His ordinances and did not walk in His statutes. They will witness the Lord's judgments on Jerusalem in the sight of all who pass by. Jerusalem will become a reproach, taunt, instruction and astonishment to them.

l: sword (the sword of judgment), The Book of Ezekiel, Chapter 5
s: The sword appears first as the prophet's razor and the instrument for striking a third of the hair around the city. It then stands for the Lord's judgment: a third of the people will fall by the sword around Jerusalem, and the Lord will draw out a sword after the scattered third. At the end He promises to bring the sword on her.

l: hair (the prophet's hair), The Book of Ezekiel, Chapter 5
s: The hair shaved from the prophet's head and beard is weighed and divided into thirds as a sign for Jerusalem's people. One third is burned in the city, one third is struck with the sword, and one third is scattered to the wind. A small number of strands is bound in his robe, and some of those are cast into the fire, from which fire will spread to all the house of Israel.

l: famine, The Book of Ezekiel, Chapter 5
s: Famine is described as a cause of death within Jerusalem, consuming a third of her people along with pestilence. The Lord calls it His evil arrows of destruction, promises to increase it, and says He will break the people's staff of bread. He lists famine first among the things He will send, together with evil animals, pestilence, blood and the sword.

l: God's judgment and wrath, The Book of Ezekiel, Chapter 5
s: The Lord announces judgments on Jerusalem that He has never done before and will never do again, because of her abominations and the defilement of His sanctuary. His eye will not spare and He will have no pity, until His anger is accomplished and His wrath rests. Through this the people will know that the LORD has spoken in His zeal.

l: The Book of Ezekiel, The Book of Ezekiel, Chapter 6
s: The LORD commands the son of man to set his face toward the mountains of Israel and prophesy judgment against them. The Lord GOD declares he will bring a sword, destroy the high places, break the altars and incense altars, and strew the slain and bones of the children of Israel before their idols. Yet he promises to leave a remnant who escape among the nations, remember him, and loathe themselves for their idolatry. The son of man is told to strike his hand, stamp his foot, and cry "Alas!" over Israel's abominations, since the people will die by sword, famine, and pestilence according to their distance or circumstance. The LORD says he will make the land desolate from the wilderness toward Diblah, so that they will know that he is the LORD.

l: the LORD, The Book of Ezekiel, Chapter 6
s: The Lord GOD commands the son of man to prophesy against the mountains of Israel and announces that he will bring a sword, destroy the high places, and lay the slain before their idols. He will leave a remnant, and he has been broken by his people's lewd hearts and eyes. Through these judgments, including making the land desolate toward Diblah, they will know that he is the LORD.

l: Ezekiel, The Book of Ezekiel, Chapter 6
s: The son of man is told to set his face toward the mountains of Israel and prophesy to them the word of the Lord GOD. He is also told to strike with his hand, stamp with his foot, and say "Alas!" because of the abominations of the house of Israel.

l: mountains of Israel, The Book of Ezekiel, Chapter 6
s: The mountains of Israel, along with the hills, watercourses, and valleys, are addressed by the prophecy and told to hear the word of the Lord GOD. A sword will come on them, and the slain will lie among the idols on every high hill and on all the mountaintops.

l: Israel, The Book of Ezekiel, Chapter 6
s: Israel, called the children of Israel and the house of Israel, will see its dead bodies laid before its idols and its cities laid waste. Some will escape as a remnant among the nations, but others will fall by sword, famine, and pestilence, and the land will become desolate and waste.

l: idols (Israel's idols), The Book of Ezekiel, Chapter 6
s: Israel's idols will be broken and cease, and the slain will be cast down and the bones scattered before and around them. They are the objects after which the people's eyes play the prostitute and to which pleasant aroma was offered.

l: high places (of Israel), The Book of Ezekiel, Chapter 6
s: The Lord GOD says he will destroy the high places and that they will be desolate. They are linked to the altars and incense altars that will be laid waste, broken, and cut down.

l: remnant (of Israel), The Book of Ezekiel, Chapter 6
s: The Lord will leave a remnant who escape the sword among the nations when Israel is scattered. In captivity they will remember him, recognize how he was broken by their lewd hearts and idolatrous eyes, loathe themselves for their abominations, and know that he is the LORD.

l: sword, famine, and pestilence, The Book of Ezekiel, Chapter 6
s: These are the means by which Israel will fall: the far off will die of pestilence, the near will fall by the sword, and the besieged remnant in the city will die by famine. Through them the Lord says he will accomplish his wrath.

l: abominations and defilement of the sanctuary, The Book of Ezekiel, Chapter 6
s: Israel's idolatry is described as evil abominations, including a lewd heart that departed from the Lord, eyes that play the prostitute after idols, and offering pleasant aroma on high hills and under green trees and oaks. It is the cause of the coming judgment and the reason the survivors will loathe themselves.

l: The Book of Ezekiel, The Book of Ezekiel, Chapter 7
s: In Ezekiel 7, the LORD tells the prophet, called 'son of man', to announce to the land of Israel that the end has come on its four corners. The LORD declares he will pour out his anger, judge the people according to their ways, and bring their abominations upon them without pity, so that they will know he is the LORD. The coming day brings tumult, with the sword outside and pestilence and famine within, leaving survivors moaning on the mountains like doves, with weak hands, sackcloth, shame, and baldness. Silver and gold become unclean and cannot deliver them, and the LORD gives their treasured ornament and holy places to strangers and the wicked of the earth, who profane them. With the land full of bloody crimes and violence, the worst of the nations will possess their houses, rumor will pile on rumor, the law will perish from the priest, and the king, prince, and people will mourn and be troubled.

l: the LORD, The Book of Ezekiel, Chapter 7
s: The LORD commands the prophet to speak and declares he will send his anger, pour out his wrath, judge the people according to their ways, and show no pity. He turns his face from them, hands their treasures and holy places to strangers, and says that through this they will know he is the LORD.

l: land of Israel, The Book of Ezekiel, Chapter 7
s: The land of Israel is told that the end has come on its four corners. It is described as full of bloody crimes and violence, and its houses and holy places will be taken and profaned by the worst of the nations.

l: the end (coming doom), The Book of Ezekiel, Chapter 7
s: The end is announced repeatedly as a unique disaster that has come, awakes against the land, and is near, a day of tumult rather than joyful shouting. The rod has blossomed and pride has budded, and the vision concerns the whole multitude, so none will return or remain.

l: abominations and iniquity, The Book of Ezekiel, Chapter 7
s: The abominations of the people are to be brought on them and will be among them as part of the LORD's judgment. The people made images of their abominations and detestable things in the ornament of beauty the LORD had set in majesty, so he has made it unclean to them.

l: inhabitants of Israel, The Book of Ezekiel, Chapter 7
s: The inhabitants are warned that their doom has come, and they are to be judged according to their ways. Buyer and seller alike face wrath, no one goes to battle despite the trumpet, and survivors moan on the mountains with feeble hands, sackcloth, shame, and baldness. They seek peace and a vision from the prophet but find none, as the law perishes from the priest and counsel from the elders, and the king and prince mourn.

l: strangers and wicked nations, The Book of Ezekiel, Chapter 7
s: The LORD gives the ornament into the hands of strangers as prey and to the wicked of the earth as plunder, and they profane it. He will bring the worst of the nations to possess the people's houses, and robbers will enter and profane his secret place.

l: The Book of Ezekiel, The Book of Ezekiel, Chapter 8
s: In the sixth year, on the fifth day of the sixth month, Ezekiel sits in his house with the elders of Judah when the Lord GOD's hand falls on him. A fiery figure lifts him by a lock of his head in visions to Jerusalem, where he is shown a series of escalating abominations. He sees the image of jealousy at the north gate, seventy elders of Israel burning incense before idols and creeping things portrayed on a hidden chamber wall, women weeping for Tammuz at the north gate of the LORD's house, and about twenty-five men worshiping the sun with their backs to the LORD's temple. The Lord declares that Judah has filled the land with violence and provoked him, and that he will deal in wrath, showing no pity and refusing to hear their cries.

l: Ezekiel, The Book of Ezekiel, Chapter 8
s: Ezekiel sits in his house with the elders of Judah when the Lord GOD's hand falls on him, and he is lifted by a lock of his head in visions of God to Jerusalem. He is told to look, dig through a wall, and enter, and is repeatedly asked 'do you see?' as he witnesses successive abominations.

l: the LORD, The Book of Ezekiel, Chapter 8
s: The Lord GOD's hand falls on Ezekiel, and a fiery figure brings him in visions to Jerusalem to show him the abominations of Israel. He says the people's acts drive him far from his sanctuary, and he declares he will deal in wrath, not spare or pity, and not hear their cries.

l: Jerusalem, The Book of Ezekiel, Chapter 8
s: Jerusalem is where the Spirit brings Ezekiel in visions of God, to the door of the gate of the inner court facing north. There he sees idolatry in the gate, the court, and the temple precincts.

l: image of jealousy, The Book of Ezekiel, Chapter 8
s: The image of jealousy stands at the door of the gate of the inner court facing north, in the entry northward of the gate of the altar. It is described as provoking to jealousy and is the first of the great abominations Ezekiel is shown.

l: house of Israel, The Book of Ezekiel, Chapter 8
s: The house of Israel is said to commit great abominations at the sanctuary, driving the Lord to go far off from it. Its idols are portrayed on the wall of a hidden chamber, and its elders worship in the dark.

l: seventy elders of Israel, The Book of Ezekiel, Chapter 8
s: Seventy men of the elders of the house of Israel stand before the portrayed idols, each with a censer, with Jaazaniah the son of Shaphan in their midst, as incense smoke rises. The Lord says they act in the dark in rooms of imagery, saying 'The LORD doesn't see us. The LORD has forsaken the land.'

l: women weeping for Tammuz, The Book of Ezekiel, Chapter 8
s: Ezekiel sees women sitting at the door of the north gate of the LORD's house weeping for Tammuz. The Lord names this as an abomination and says greater ones are still to come.

l: twenty-five men sun worshipers, The Book of Ezekiel, Chapter 8
s: About twenty-five men stand in the inner court between the porch and the altar at the door of the LORD's temple. Their backs are toward the temple and their faces toward the east, and they worship the sun.

l: idols and creeping things (portrayed on the wall), The Book of Ezekiel, Chapter 8
s: Through a hole Ezekiel dug in the wall and a door beyond it, he sees every form of creeping things, abominable animals, and all the idols of the house of Israel portrayed around the wall. The seventy elders stand before them offering incense.

l: the temple, The Book of Ezekiel, Chapter 8
s: The LORD's house has a north gate, an inner court, and a temple door between the porch and the altar, all sites of idolatry in this vision. The Lord says the abominations drive him far from his sanctuary, and the glory of the God of Israel is present in the scene.

l: abominations and defilement of the sanctuary, The Book of Ezekiel, Chapter 8
s: The Lord shows Ezekiel a progression of abominations: the image of jealousy, idols and creeping things in a hidden chamber, women weeping for Tammuz, and sun worship at the temple door. Each is followed by a promise of greater ones, and the Lord says Judah has also filled the land with violence.

l: God's wrath and judgment, The Book of Ezekiel, Chapter 8
s: The Lord declares he will deal in wrath, his eye will not spare, and he will have no pity. Though the people cry in his ears with a loud voice, he will not hear them.

l: The Book of Ezekiel, The Book of Ezekiel, Chapter 9
s: In this chapter the LORD summons those in charge of the city, and six men with destroying weapons arrive with one man clothed in linen carrying a writer's inkhorn, and they stand beside the bronze altar. The LORD's glory moves from the cherub to the threshold of the house, and he commands the man in linen to mark the foreheads of those who sigh and cry over the city's abominations. He orders the other six to follow and kill the old, young, virgins, children and women without pity, sparing anyone marked, beginning at his sanctuary with the old men before the house. The narrator, left alone, falls on his face and asks whether all the remnant of Israel will be destroyed. The LORD answers that the iniquity of Israel and Judah is great, the land full of blood and the city full of perversion, and he will bring their way on their heads; the man in linen then reports that he has done as commanded.

l: the LORD, The Book of Ezekiel, Chapter 9
s: The LORD summons the city's overseers and commands the man in linen to mark the mourners, and the six men to kill without pity everyone unmarked, beginning at his sanctuary. He answers the narrator's plea by citing the great iniquity of Israel and Judah, the blood in the land and the people's claim that he has forsaken it and doesn't see, and says his eye won't spare nor will he pity them.

l: man clothed in linen, The Book of Ezekiel, Chapter 9
s: The man clothed in linen, with a writer's inkhorn at his side, comes with the six men and stands beside the bronze altar. He is told to go through Jerusalem and mark the foreheads of those who sigh and cry over the abominations, and he afterward reports that he has done as commanded.

l: six men (the executioners), The Book of Ezekiel, Chapter 9
s: Six men come from the way of the upper gate toward the north, each with a slaughter weapon in hand, and stand beside the bronze altar. They are ordered to follow the man in linen through the city and kill utterly without sparing or pity, defile the house and fill the courts with the slain, avoiding anyone with the mark. They begin with the old men before the house and strike in the city.

l: Jerusalem, The Book of Ezekiel, Chapter 9
s: Jerusalem is the city through which the man in linen goes to mark people and through which the six men strike. It is described as full of perversion, with the land full of blood, and its people say the LORD has forsaken the land and doesn't see. The LORD's wrath is being poured out on it.

l: Israel, The Book of Ezekiel, Chapter 9
s: The house of Israel, together with Judah, is judged to have exceedingly great iniquity. The narrator fears that the LORD will destroy all the residue of Israel in pouring out his wrath on Jerusalem, and the LORD replies that he will bring their way on their head.

l: mark, The Book of Ezekiel, Chapter 9
s: The mark is set on the foreheads of the men who sigh and cry over the abominations in the city, by the man clothed in linen. The six men are commanded not to come near anyone on whom the mark is found.

l: men who sigh and cry, The Book of Ezekiel, Chapter 9
s: These men sigh and cry over all the abominations done within Jerusalem. The LORD orders them marked on the forehead, which sets them apart so that the executioners do not come near them.

l: slaughter of the city, The Book of Ezekiel, Chapter 9
s: The six men carry out the slaughter, killing old men, young men, virgins, little children and women, beginning at the old men before the house and filling the courts with the slain. The narrator, left alive, falls on his face and cries out in protest. The LORD justifies it by the people's iniquity and bloodshed.

l: The Book of Ezekiel, The Book of Ezekiel, Chapter 10
s: The narrator sees a sapphire-like throne in the expanse above the cherubim. The speaker commands the man clothed in linen to go between the whirling wheels and take coals of fire from between the cherubim to scatter over the city; a cherub puts the fire into his hands and he goes out. The narrator describes the cherubim and the four wheels beside them, which are full of eyes, move in four directions without turning, and are moved by the spirit of the living creature. Each cherub has four faces (cherub, man, lion, eagle) and four wings, and the narrator identifies them as the living creature he saw by the river Chebar. The LORD's glory rises from the cherub to the threshold of the house, which fills with cloud and brightness, then leaves the threshold and stands over the cherubim, which rise up and stop at the east gate of the LORD's house with the glory of the God of Israel above them.

l: the LORD, The Book of Ezekiel, Chapter 10
s: The LORD's glory mounts up from the cherub and stands over the threshold of the house, filling it with cloud and brightness. It then goes out from the threshold, stands over the cherubim, and rests above them at the east gate of the LORD's house, where it is called the glory of the God of Israel.

l: cherubim, The Book of Ezekiel, Chapter 10
s: The cherubim stand on the right side of the house, and one cherub hands fire from between them to the man clothed in linen. Each has four faces (cherub, man, lion, eagle), four wings, and human-like hands under the wings, and the narrator identifies them with the living creature he saw by the river Chebar. They mount up from the earth with the wheels beside them and stop at the east gate of the LORD's house.

l: man clothed in linen, The Book of Ezekiel, Chapter 10
s: He is commanded to go in between the whirling wheels, under the cherub, and fill his hands with coals of fire to scatter over the city. He goes in and stands beside a wheel, receives the fire from the cherub's hand, and goes out.

l: wheels (beside the living creatures), The Book of Ezekiel, Chapter 10
s: Four wheels, one beside each cherub, look like beryl stone, each like a wheel within a wheel, and are full of eyes all around. They go in four directions without turning, and they move, stand, and mount up with the cherubim because the spirit of the living creature is in them. They are called "the whirling wheels" in the narrator's hearing.

l: coals of fire, The Book of Ezekiel, Chapter 10
s: The man clothed in linen is told to take coals of fire from between the cherubim and scatter them over the city. A cherub stretches out his hand to the fire between the cherubim, takes some, and puts it into the man's hands.

l: the temple, The Book of Ezekiel, Chapter 10
s: The house is filled with the cloud, and its court is full of the brightness of the LORD's glory, while the sound of the cherubim's wings is heard to the outer court. The LORD's glory leaves the threshold of the house, and the cherubim stop at the door of its east gate.

l: The Book of Ezekiel, The Book of Ezekiel, Chapter 11
s: The Spirit brings Ezekiel to the LORD's east gate, where he sees twenty-five men, including the princes Jaazaniah son of Azzur and Pelatiah son of Benaiah, who give wicked counsel in the city and claim they are the meat in the cauldron. Ezekiel is told to prophesy against them: the LORD says the slain they have multiplied are the meat, and the men will be brought out, delivered to strangers, and judged at the border of Israel. Pelatiah dies as Ezekiel prophesies, and Ezekiel cries out asking whether the remnant of Israel will be fully ended. The LORD answers that He will be a sanctuary to the scattered exiles, gather them, give them the land of Israel, and give them one heart and a new spirit, while those devoted to detestable things will bear the consequences. The LORD's glory then leaves the city and stands on the mountain east of it, and Ezekiel, carried back to the captives in Chaldea, tells them everything he was shown.

l: the LORD, The Book of Ezekiel, Chapter 11
s: The LORD identifies the twenty-five men as devisers of iniquity and commands Ezekiel to prophesy judgment against them, promising to bring the sword on them and judge them at the border of Israel. He answers Ezekiel's lament by promising to be a sanctuary to the scattered, to gather them, give them the land, and give them one heart and a new spirit. His glory rises with the cherubim and wheels, leaves the middle of the city, and stands on the mountain east of it.

l: Ezekiel, The Book of Ezekiel, Chapter 11
s: Ezekiel is lifted by the Spirit to the east gate of the LORD's house, where he sees the twenty-five men and is told to prophesy against them. When Pelatiah dies, he falls on his face and cries out asking whether the LORD will make a full end of the remnant of Israel. The Spirit then carries him in the vision to the captives in Chaldea, and he tells them all that the LORD showed him.

l: Pelatiah the son of Benaiah, The Book of Ezekiel, Chapter 11
s: Pelatiah is seen among the twenty-five men at the east gate and is named, with Jaazaniah, as a prince of the people. He dies while Ezekiel is prophesying.

l: twenty-five men, The Book of Ezekiel, Chapter 11
s: The twenty-five men stand at the door of the east gate, and are described as those who devise iniquity and give wicked counsel in the city. They say the time is not near to build houses and that the city is the cauldron and they are the meat. The LORD declares they will be brought out, delivered to strangers, and judged by the sword at the border of Israel.

l: house of Israel, The Book of Ezekiel, Chapter 11
s: The house of Israel is said to know the thoughts the LORD knows in their minds, and is charged with not walking in His statutes or keeping His ordinances but following the ordinances of surrounding nations. The LORD promises to gather them, give them one heart and a new spirit in place of the stony heart, so they may walk in His statutes and be His people. Those whose hearts follow detestable things will have their way brought on their own heads.

l: inhabitants of Jerusalem, The Book of Ezekiel, Chapter 11
s: The inhabitants of Jerusalem have told Ezekiel's brothers and all the house of Israel to go far away from the LORD, claiming the land has been given to them as a possession.

l: the exiles (Ezekiel's brothers), The Book of Ezekiel, Chapter 11
s: Ezekiel's brothers and relatives, the whole house of Israel, are those the inhabitants of Jerusalem told to go far from the LORD. The LORD says He removed and scattered them among the nations but will be a sanctuary to them for a little while there. He promises to gather them and give them the land of Israel, and Ezekiel finally relays the vision to the captives in Chaldea.

l: Jerusalem, The Book of Ezekiel, Chapter 11
s: The city is where the twenty-five men give wicked counsel and where the slain have been multiplied and fill the streets. The LORD says the slain are the meat and the city the cauldron, but the men will be brought out of it. His glory goes up from the middle of the city and stands on the mountain on its east side.

l: land of Israel, The Book of Ezekiel, Chapter 11
s: The inhabitants of Jerusalem claim the land as their possession, but the LORD promises to give the land of Israel to the gathered exiles. When they come there, they will remove all its detestable things and abominations.

l: cauldron and meat saying, The Book of Ezekiel, Chapter 11
s: The twenty-five men say, 'This is the cauldron, and we are the meat,' while dismissing the time for building houses. The LORD reverses it, saying their slain are the meat and the city the cauldron, and that the men will not be the meat but will be brought out and judged at the border of Israel.

l: The Book of Ezekiel, The Book of Ezekiel, Chapter 12
s: In Ezekiel 12, the LORD tells Ezekiel, the son of man living among a rebellious house, to act out an exile by packing baggage, digging through a wall, and carrying his things out in the dark with his face covered. Ezekiel does so, and the LORD explains that the act is a sign concerning the prince in Jerusalem and the house of Israel, who will go into exile, with the prince captured in a net and brought to Babylon, where he will die without seeing it. The LORD says a few will be spared so they can declare their abominations among the nations. Ezekiel is also told to eat and drink with trembling as a sign of the fear that will come on Jerusalem's inhabitants and the desolation of the land. Finally, the LORD declares an end to the proverb that visions fail and are far off, saying his word will be performed without delay.

l: the LORD, The Book of Ezekiel, Chapter 12
s: The LORD commands Ezekiel to enact the moving-out sign and then explains its meaning to the house of Israel. He declares that he will spread his net on the prince, scatter his helpers, draw out the sword after them, and leave a few survivors so that all will know he is the LORD. He also announces that he will end the proverb about failing visions and perform his word without delay.

l: Ezekiel, The Book of Ezekiel, Chapter 12
s: Ezekiel, addressed as son of man, is told he dwells among a rebellious house that sees and hears but does not perceive. He obeys the commands to bring out his baggage by day, dig through the wall in the evening, and carry it on his shoulder in the dark. He is also told to eat and drink with trembling, and to deliver the LORD's messages about the exile, the desolation, and the proverb. He is called a sign to the house of Israel.

l: house of Israel, The Book of Ezekiel, Chapter 12
s: The house of Israel is described as a rebellious house with eyes and ears that do not see or hear. They ask Ezekiel what he is doing, and are told that the act concerns the prince in Jerusalem and all Israel among whom he is. They will go into exile and be scattered among the nations, and they are quoted as saying the vision is for many days off.

l: prince in Jerusalem, The Book of Ezekiel, Chapter 12
s: The prince is the subject of the burden the LORD explains. He will carry his baggage on his shoulder in the dark, go out through a hole dug in the wall, and cover his face so he will not see the land. The LORD will catch him in a net and snare and bring him to Babylon, the land of the Chaldeans, where he will die without seeing it. His helpers and bands will be scattered to every wind.

l: exile, The Book of Ezekiel, Chapter 12
s: Exile is what Ezekiel's actions portray, as he goes out at evening like men going into exile. The LORD says the house of Israel will go into exile and captivity, dispersed among the nations and scattered through the countries. A few will be left from sword, famine, and pestilence to declare their abominations among the nations.

l: baggage (Ezekiel's baggage), The Book of Ezekiel, Chapter 12
s: Ezekiel prepares baggage for moving, brings it out by day in the sight of the people, and then carries it out on his shoulder in the dark through a hole dug in the wall. It serves as the physical prop of the sign, matching what the prince will do when he leaves with his baggage.

l: sign act of moving out, The Book of Ezekiel, Chapter 12
s: The sign act is Ezekiel's moving out in the sight of the people, with baggage by day, a wall dug through in the evening, and his face covered. He does as commanded, and the LORD explains in the morning that it means, 'I am your sign. As I have done, so will it be done to them.' It foretells the exile of the prince and the people.

l: proverb about prolonged days and failing visions, The Book of Ezekiel, Chapter 12
s: The proverb in the land of Israel says, 'The days are prolonged, and every vision fails.' The LORD says he will make it cease so it is no longer used in Israel. He replaces it with the declaration that the days are at hand and the fulfillment of every vision is near.

l: fulfillment of the LORD's word, The Book of Ezekiel, Chapter 12
s: The LORD declares that the days are at hand for the fulfillment of every vision, with no more false vision or flattering divination in Israel. He says the word he speaks will be performed and will no longer be deferred, but will be carried out in the days of the rebellious house. He repeats that none of his words will be delayed any more.

l: The Book of Ezekiel, The Book of Ezekiel, Chapter 13
s: The LORD commands Ezekiel, called son of man, to prophesy against the prophets of Israel who speak from their own spirit and have seen nothing, and who claim 'The LORD says' though he has not sent them. They are compared to foxes in waste places, they did not repair the gaps in the wall, and they promised 'Peace' when there was none, plastering a flimsy wall with whitewash. The LORD declares that a stormy wind, flooding shower and hailstones will bring the wall down and consume those who plastered it. Ezekiel is then told to set his face against the women who prophesy from their own heart and sew magic bands and veils to hunt souls for handfuls of barley and pieces of bread. The LORD vows to tear off these bands and veils, free his people from their hands, and end false visions and divination, so that they will know he is the LORD.

l: the LORD, The Book of Ezekiel, Chapter 13
s: The LORD speaks to Ezekiel and declares that he has not sent the prophets who say 'The LORD says.' He announces that he is against them, that his hand will be against them, and that they will be excluded from the council of his people, the writing of the house of Israel, and the land of Israel. He vows to bring down the whitewashed wall in wrath, to tear the women's magic bands and veils and free his people from their hands, and he repeatedly says that people will then know he is the LORD.

l: Ezekiel, The Book of Ezekiel, Chapter 13
s: Ezekiel, addressed as son of man, receives the LORD's word and is told to prophesy against the prophets of Israel who speak out of their own heart. He is also told to set his face against the women who prophesy from their own heart and to deliver the LORD's message of judgment against them.

l: Israel, The Book of Ezekiel, Chapter 13
s: Israel is the people and house whose prophets have been like foxes in waste places and have led them astray by proclaiming peace where there is none. The LORD says he will deliver his people from the hands of those who ensnare them. He also says the false prophets will not be written in the writing of the house of Israel or enter the land of Israel.

l: false prophets of Israel, The Book of Ezekiel, Chapter 13
s: The prophets of Israel follow their own spirit, have seen nothing, and claim 'The LORD says' though the LORD has not sent them. They did not go up into the gaps or build up the wall, and they seduced the people by saying 'Peace' and plastering the wall with whitewash. The LORD declares he is against them, that they will be consumed when the wall falls, and that they will lose their place in the council, the register, and the land of Israel.

l: women who prophesy (daughters of your people), The Book of Ezekiel, Chapter 13
s: These women prophesy out of their own heart and sew magic bands on elbows and make veils for heads to hunt souls. They profaned the LORD among his people for handfuls of barley and pieces of bread, killing souls who should not die and saving alive those who should not live through lies. The LORD says he will tear off their bands and veils, release the souls they ensnared like birds, and end their false visions and divination.

l: whitewashed wall, The Book of Ezekiel, Chapter 13
s: The wall is built by the people and plastered with whitewash by the false prophets, standing for the false assurance of peace. The LORD says it will fall under a storm, its foundation will be uncovered, and those who plastered it will be consumed within it. It will be said to them, 'Where is the plaster with which you have plastered it?' and the LORD says the wall and its plasterers will be no more.

l: storm of judgment, The Book of Ezekiel, Chapter 13
s: The LORD announces a stormy wind, an overflowing shower and great hailstones as the instruments of his wrath and anger against the whitewashed wall. The storm will tear down the wall, bring it to the ground, and consume the false prophets in the midst of it, so that they will know he is the LORD.

l: false visions and lying divination, The Book of Ezekiel, Chapter 13
s: The prophets and the women are charged with seeing falsehood and speaking lying divination, claiming the LORD's authority when he has not spoken. These false visions led people to hope that the word would be confirmed and to believe in peace. The LORD promises that the women will no more see false visions or practice divination, and that his hand will be against the prophets who utter them.

l: magic bands and veils, The Book of Ezekiel, Chapter 13
s: The women sew magic bands on all elbows and make veils for the heads of people of every stature in order to hunt souls. The LORD says he is against the bands, will tear them from the women's arms, and will tear the veils. He will let the ensnared souls fly free like birds and deliver his people out of the women's hands.

l: The Book of Ezekiel, The Book of Ezekiel, Chapter 14
s: Elders of Israel come to the speaker, and the LORD tells him they have taken idols into their hearts and set their iniquity before them, so he will answer them according to their many idols and calls the house of Israel to return from idols. Anyone, Israelite or stranger, who does this and then inquires of a prophet will be answered by the LORD himself, set apart as a sign and proverb, and cut off; a deceived prophet is destroyed too, and both bear their iniquity. The LORD then says that when a land sins and he sends famine, evil animals, sword, or pestilence, even Noah, Daniel, and Job would save only their own souls and no sons or daughters. He declares that these four severe judgments will come on Jerusalem, yet a remnant of sons and daughters will be carried out and will comfort the speaker's audience, showing that the LORD acted not without cause.

l: the LORD, The Book of Ezekiel, Chapter 14
s: The LORD refuses to be freely inquired of by men who harbor idols, declaring he will answer them himself according to their idols and set his face against them. He declares that a sinning land will be judged and that even the righteousness of Noah, Daniel, and Job could not save others. He will send four severe judgments on Jerusalem, leave a remnant, and show that he did nothing without cause.

l: Ezekiel, The Book of Ezekiel, Chapter 14
s: Addressed as 'son of man', he is visited by elders of Israel and receives two words from the LORD, one about idolatrous inquirers and one about the land's judgment. He is told that the remnant carried out will come to him, and that he will see their ways and be comforted.

l: elders of Israel, The Book of Ezekiel, Chapter 14
s: Some of the elders come and sit before the speaker. The LORD says these men have taken idols into their hearts and put their iniquity's stumbling block before their faces, so he questions whether he should be inquired of by them.

l: house of Israel, The Book of Ezekiel, Chapter 14
s: The house of Israel is described as estranged from the LORD through its idols, and is called to return and turn away from its abominations. The LORD's aim is that they no longer go astray or defile themselves, but be his people with him as their God.

l: idols, The Book of Ezekiel, Chapter 14
s: Idols are taken into the hearts of Israelites and become the stumbling block of their iniquity. The LORD says he will answer idolatrous inquirers according to the multitude of their idols, and calls Israel to turn from them.

l: prophet (who is inquired of), The Book of Ezekiel, Chapter 14
s: The prophet is the one to whom idolatrous men come to inquire. If a prophet is deceived and speaks a word, the LORD says he himself deceived him and will stretch out his hand to destroy him, so that the prophet's iniquity matches that of the one who seeks him.

l: Noah, The Book of Ezekiel, Chapter 14
s: Noah is named as one of three righteous men who, if present in a sinning land under judgment, would deliver only their own souls by their righteousness. They would save neither sons nor daughters.

l: Daniel, The Book of Ezekiel, Chapter 14
s: Daniel is named alongside Noah and Job as a righteous man. If in a land facing famine, evil animals, sword, or pestilence, he would deliver only his own soul and not any sons or daughters.

l: Job, The Book of Ezekiel, Chapter 14
s: Job is named with Noah and Daniel as a righteous man whose righteousness would save only himself in a land under the LORD's judgment, not his children.

l: sinful land, The Book of Ezekiel, Chapter 14
s: A land that sins by trespass is hypothetically struck by the LORD, who breaks its bread supply and cuts off man and animal through famine, evil animals, sword, or pestilence. Even the presence of three righteous men would not spare it; only they would be delivered while the land became desolate.

l: Jerusalem, The Book of Ezekiel, Chapter 14
s: The LORD says he will send all four of his severe judgments on Jerusalem to cut off man and animal. A remnant will nonetheless be left in it and carried out, and its evil will be understood as not without cause.

l: sword, famine, and pestilence, The Book of Ezekiel, Chapter 14
s: The four severe judgments are the sword, the famine, the evil animals, and the pestilence. Each is described as something the LORD sends on a sinning land, and he says he will send all four on Jerusalem to cut off man and animal.

l: remnant, The Book of Ezekiel, Chapter 14
s: A remnant of sons and daughters will be left in Jerusalem and carried out of it. They will come to the speaker's audience, and when their way and doings are seen, the audience will be comforted and know the LORD acted with cause.

l: The Book of Ezekiel, The Book of Ezekiel, Chapter 15
s: The LORD's word comes to a 'son of man' with a question about the vine tree: what makes its wood better than that of any other forest tree? The wood is useless for making anything, not even a pin to hang a vessel on, and once the fire has burned both its ends and its middle it is even less useful. The LORD applies this to the inhabitants of Jerusalem, saying he will give them to the fire as he gave the vine wood. He will set his face against them so that the fire still devours them, and they will know he is the LORD. He will make the land desolate because they have acted unfaithfully.

l: the LORD, The Book of Ezekiel, Chapter 15
s: The LORD speaks to the 'son of man' and compares Jerusalem's inhabitants to useless vine wood. He declares he will set his face against them and give them to the fire. He says that through this they will know he is the LORD, and that he will make the land desolate because of their unfaithfulness.

l: vine tree, The Book of Ezekiel, Chapter 15
s: The vine tree, and its branch among the forest trees, is shown to be worthless for any work: nothing can be made from its wood, not even a pin to hang a vessel on. It is cast into the fire for fuel, and the fire devours both ends and the middle. It serves as the comparison for the inhabitants of Jerusalem.

l: fire, The Book of Ezekiel, Chapter 15
s: The fire devours the vine wood at both ends and in the middle, leaving it burned and even less useful. The LORD says he has given the vine wood to the fire and will likewise give the inhabitants of Jerusalem. Though they go out from the fire, it will still devour them.

l: inhabitants of Jerusalem, The Book of Ezekiel, Chapter 15
s: The inhabitants of Jerusalem are likened to the useless vine wood given to the fire. The LORD will set his face against them, and though they go out from the fire, it will still devour them. They will then know that he is the LORD.

l: land, The Book of Ezekiel, Chapter 15
s: The LORD says he will make the land desolate. The reason given is that the inhabitants have acted unfaithfully.

l: The Book of Ezekiel, The Book of Ezekiel, Chapter 16
s: In Ezekiel 16 the Lord GOD tells Ezekiel to make Jerusalem know her abominations. He recounts how she was born of a Canaanite land with an Amorite father and Hittite mother, cast out and abhorred, then rescued, made to live, adorned, and covenanted to him. She trusted in her beauty, made high places and images from the gifts he gave her, prostituted herself with Egyptians, Assyrians and Chaldeans, and sacrificed her children. The Lord GOD declares he will gather her lovers to strip, stone, and burn her, and compares her to her sisters Samaria and Sodom, whom she has outdone in corruption. He nevertheless promises to restore all three sisters, remember his covenant, and establish an everlasting covenant so she will know he is the LORD, when he has forgiven her.

l: Jerusalem, The Book of Ezekiel, Chapter 16
s: Jerusalem is described as born to an Amorite father and Hittite mother, cast out at birth, then saved, adorned, and made the Lord GOD's own. She trusted in her beauty, practiced prostitution with many nations, and killed her children for idols, so she is judged more corrupt than Samaria and Sodom. She is promised eventual restoration, an everlasting covenant, and forgiveness, leaving her ashamed and silent.

l: the LORD, The Book of Ezekiel, Chapter 16
s: The Lord GOD recounts that he found Jerusalem abandoned in her blood, told her to live, made her grow, covenanted with her, and adorned her. He pronounces judgment through her lovers for her unfaithfulness, then promises to remember his covenant, establish an everlasting covenant, and forgive her all she has done.

l: Samaria, The Book of Ezekiel, Chapter 16
s: Samaria is Jerusalem's elder sister, dwelling at her left hand with her daughters. She has not committed half of Jerusalem's sins, and her captivity and that of her daughters will be reversed so they return to their former estate.

l: Sodom, The Book of Ezekiel, Chapter 16
s: Sodom is Jerusalem's younger sister, dwelling at her right hand with her daughters. Her iniquity was pride, fullness of bread, prosperous ease, and not strengthening the poor and needy; she was arrogant, committed abomination, and was taken away. Jerusalem has done worse than Sodom, whose captivity will be reversed and who will return to her former estate.

l: Jerusalem's lovers, The Book of Ezekiel, Chapter 16
s: Jerusalem's lovers include the Egyptians, Assyrians, Chaldeans, and others to whom she gave gifts and bribes. The Lord GOD says he will gather them against her, and they will uncover her nakedness, tear down her high places, strip her jewels and clothes, stone her, pierce her with swords, and burn her houses.

l: idols and images, The Book of Ezekiel, Chapter 16
s: Jerusalem made high places and images of men from the garments and gold and silver jewels the Lord GOD gave her. She set his oil, incense, and bread before them and sacrificed her children to them. The blood of her children given to these idols is named as a reason for judgment.

l: covenant between God and Jerusalem, The Book of Ezekiel, Chapter 16
s: The Lord GOD pledged himself to Jerusalem and entered a covenant with her when he covered her nakedness, and she became his. She despised the oath and broke the covenant, yet he promises to remember it from her youth and establish an everlasting covenant, not by her covenant, so that she will know he is the LORD.

l: Jerusalem's prostitution (idolatry), The Book of Ezekiel, Chapter 16
s: Jerusalem's prostitution is depicted as idolatry and unfaithfulness, in which she built lofty places at every street, opened her feet to every passerby, and sought out Egyptians, Assyrians, and Chaldeans. She was insatiable and unlike ordinary prostitutes because she paid her lovers rather than being paid. It also included child sacrifice, and her filthiness and idols are given as grounds for judgment.

l: Judgment on Jerusalem, The Book of Ezekiel, Chapter 16
s: The Lord GOD declares that he will judge Jerusalem as women who break wedlock and shed blood are judged. Her lovers will strip her, destroy her high places, stone her, stab her, and burn her houses, ending her prostitution and appeasing his wrath and jealousy. The judgment is followed by promises of restoration and forgiveness.

l: The Book of Ezekiel, The Book of Ezekiel, Chapter 17
s: The LORD tells Ezekiel to give the house of Israel a riddle about two great eagles, a cedar, and a vine. The first eagle takes the top of Lebanon's cedar to a city of merchants and plants seed in fertile soil, where it becomes a low spreading vine; the vine then turns toward a second eagle, and the LORD asks whether it will prosper. The LORD explains that the king of Babylon took Jerusalem's king and princes, made a covenant and oath with one of the royal offspring, but that king rebelled by sending ambassadors to Egypt for horses and troops. The LORD vows that this king will die in Babylon, that Pharaoh's army will not help him, and that his broken oath and covenant will fall on his own head. The chapter closes with the LORD promising to plant a tender twig from the cedar's top on Israel's high mountain, where it will become a good cedar sheltering birds, so that all the trees will know the LORD has spoken and acted.

l: the LORD, The Book of Ezekiel, Chapter 17
s: The Lord GOD gives Ezekiel a riddle and parable and then interprets it, declaring that he will bring the despised oath and covenant on the rebel king's head, spread his net on him, and judge him in Babylon. He also promises to take a tender twig from the cedar's top and plant it on Israel's high mountain, so that all the trees will know he has spoken and done it.

l: house of Israel, The Book of Ezekiel, Chapter 17
s: The house of Israel receives the riddle and parable and is called a rebellious house that does not understand what these things mean. It is told the interpretation, and the passage ends with the promise of a good cedar planted on the mountain of Israel's height.

l: great eagle (first, Babylon's king), The Book of Ezekiel, Chapter 17
s: The first great eagle, with great wings and many-colored feathers, comes to Lebanon, takes the top of the cedar, and carries its topmost twig to a city of merchants. He also plants seed of the land in fruitful soil by many waters. It is explained as the king of Babylon, who took Jerusalem's king and princes to Babylon and made a covenant with a royal offspring.

l: great eagle (second, Pharaoh), The Book of Ezekiel, Chapter 17
s: The second great eagle, with great wings and many feathers, is the one toward whom the vine bends its roots and branches so that he might water it. In the interpretation, Pharaoh with his mighty army and great company will not help the rebel king in the war.

l: cedar (Lebanon's cedar), The Book of Ezekiel, Chapter 17
s: The top of Lebanon's cedar is taken by the first great eagle, who crops off its topmost young twig. Later the LORD himself says he will take some of the cedar's lofty top and plant a tender twig on a high mountain.

l: vine (planted by the eagle), The Book of Ezekiel, Chapter 17
s: The vine grows from seed planted by the eagle beside many waters, becoming a spreading vine of low stature whose branches turn toward the first eagle. It then bends its roots and branches toward the second eagle, and the LORD asks whether it will prosper, saying it will be pulled up and wither utterly when the east wind touches it.

l: Babylon, The Book of Ezekiel, Chapter 17
s: Babylon is the land of traffic and city of merchants where the twig is planted, and the place the king of Babylon brought Jerusalem's king and princes. The LORD declares that the rebel king will die there in the middle of Babylon, where the LORD will judge him for his trespass.

l: Judah's king (Zedekiah, royal offspring), The Book of Ezekiel, Chapter 17
s: This king is one of the royal offspring, whom the king of Babylon made a covenant with and brought under an oath so the kingdom would be brought low yet stand by keeping it. He rebelled by sending ambassadors to Egypt for horses and many people, and the LORD says he will not escape, will be taken in the LORD's snare, and will die in Babylon. His fugitives will fall by the sword and the rest will be scattered to every wind.

l: covenant and oath with Babylon, The Book of Ezekiel, Chapter 17
s: The covenant and oath were made by the king of Babylon with a royal offspring so that the kingdom might be kept low and stand by keeping the covenant. The king despised the oath and broke the covenant by seeking help from Egypt, and the LORD calls them his own oath and covenant and says he will bring them on the king's head.

l: tender twig (planted on Israel's mountain), The Book of Ezekiel, Chapter 17
s: The tender twig is cropped by the LORD from the topmost of the cedar's young twigs and planted on a high and lofty mountain, the mountain of the height of Israel. There it will produce boughs, bear fruit, become a good cedar, and give shade to birds of every kind.

l: The Book of Ezekiel, The Book of Ezekiel, Chapter 18
s: In Ezekiel 18 the Lord GOD rejects the proverb the house of Israel uses, that fathers have eaten sour grapes and the children's teeth are set on edge. He declares that all souls are his and that the soul who sins shall die. He illustrates this with a just man who lives, his robber son who dies, and that son's son who sees his father's sins, refuses to repeat them, and lives. He then says the wicked who turn from sin shall live, while the righteous who turn to iniquity shall die, answers Israel's charge that his way is unfair, and urges Israel to return, make a new heart and spirit, and live.

l: the LORD, The Book of Ezekiel, Chapter 18
s: The Lord GOD forbids Israel to use the sour grapes proverb, declares that all souls are his, and states that the soul who sins shall die. He denies any pleasure in the death of the wicked, defends his ways as fair, says he will judge each person according to his ways, and calls Israel to turn and live.

l: house of Israel, The Book of Ezekiel, Chapter 18
s: The house of Israel is rebuked for using the sour grapes proverb and for saying that the way of the Lord is not equal or fair. The Lord GOD answers that their own ways are unfair, says he will judge each of them according to his ways, and urges them to return, cast away their transgressions, and make a new heart and spirit.

l: sour grapes proverb (Israel's saying), The Book of Ezekiel, Chapter 18
s: The proverb says that the fathers have eaten sour grapes and the children's teeth are set on edge. The Lord GOD swears that Israel shall not use it any more, and the chapter answers it by teaching that each soul bears its own guilt.

l: righteous man (just man), The Book of Ezekiel, Chapter 18
s: The just man does what is lawful and right: he avoids idolatry and adultery, does not rob or wrong others, restores pledges, feeds the hungry, clothes the naked, and lends without interest. He walks in the Lord's statutes and shall surely live. The text also warns that a righteous man who turns away from his righteousness and commits iniquity will die in it, and his earlier righteous deeds will not be remembered.

l: wicked man, The Book of Ezekiel, Chapter 18
s: The wicked man who turns from all his sins, keeps the Lord's statutes, and does what is lawful and right shall surely live and not die, and his transgressions will not be remembered against him. The Lord GOD says he takes no pleasure in the death of the wicked but would rather they return from their way and live.

l: robber son (son of the just man), The Book of Ezekiel, Chapter 18
s: The son of the just man is a robber and shedder of blood who commits idolatry, adultery, oppression of the poor, and lending at interest, all of which are called abominations. He shall not live but shall surely die, and his blood will be on him. His father's righteousness does not save him.

l: righteous grandson (son of the robber), The Book of Ezekiel, Chapter 18
s: The son of the robber sees all his father's sins, fears, and does not do likewise, instead living justly by feeding the hungry, clothing the naked, and refusing interest and robbery. He shall not die for his father's iniquity but shall surely live, while his father dies in his own iniquity.

l: individual responsibility for sin, The Book of Ezekiel, Chapter 18
s: The chapter states that the soul who sins shall die, and that the son shall not bear the father's iniquity nor the father the son's. The righteousness of the righteous and the wickedness of the wicked are each on that person alone. The Lord GOD defends this as equal and fair against Israel's complaints.

l: repentance and return, The Book of Ezekiel, Chapter 18
s: The Lord GOD teaches that a wicked person who turns from all transgressions and does what is lawful and right shall live, and that none of those transgressions will be remembered. He calls Israel to return, cast away their transgressions, and make a new heart and a new spirit, so that iniquity will not be their ruin.

l: The Book of Ezekiel, The Book of Ezekiel, Chapter 19
s: Chapter 19 gives a lamentation for the princes of Israel in two images. In the first, their mother is a lioness who raises two cubs among lions; each becomes a young lion that catches prey and devours men. The nations trap the first cub in a pit and bring him with hooks to Egypt. When the lioness sees her hope lost, she raises a second cub, who lays waste cities and roars until the nations net him, cage him, and bring him to the king of Babylon so his voice is no longer heard on the mountains of Israel. In the second image, their mother is a fruitful vine planted by waters with strong branches for rulers' scepters, but it is plucked up in fury, dried by the east wind, burned by fire, and planted in a dry wilderness with no branch left to be a scepter. The text ends by declaring this a lamentation.

l: princes of Israel, The Book of Ezekiel, Chapter 19
s: The princes of Israel are the subject of the lamentation the speaker is told to take up. Their mother is described first as a lioness and then as a vine, and her fate stands for theirs.

l: lioness (mother of the princes), The Book of Ezekiel, Chapter 19
s: The lioness couches among lions and nourishes her cubs among the young lions. After the first cub is taken to Egypt she sees that she has waited and her hope is lost, so she takes another cub and makes him a young lion.

l: first cub (young lion taken to Egypt), The Book of Ezekiel, Chapter 19
s: The first cub is raised by the lioness and becomes a young lion who learns to catch prey and devours men. The nations hear of him, take him in their pit, and bring him with hooks to the land of Egypt.

l: second cub (young lion taken to Babylon), The Book of Ezekiel, Chapter 19
s: The second cub is made a young lion, goes up and down among the lions, learns to catch prey, and devours men. He knows their palaces, lays waste their cities, and desolates the land with his roaring. The nations attack him from the provinces, net and cage him with hooks, and bring him to the king of Babylon so his voice is no more heard on the mountains of Israel.

l: nations, The Book of Ezekiel, Chapter 19
s: The nations hear of the first cub, trap him in a pit, and bring him with hooks to Egypt. They later attack the second cub on every side, spread a net over him, take him in their pit, cage him, and deliver him to the king of Babylon.

l: vine (mother of the princes), The Book of Ezekiel, Chapter 19
s: The vine is planted by the waters and is fruitful and full of branches, with strong branches for the scepters of rulers and great height. It is then plucked up in fury and cast to the ground, its fruit dried by the east wind and its branches broken, withered, and consumed by fire. It is now planted in a dry and thirsty wilderness, with no strong branch left to be a scepter to rule.

l: lamentation for the princes of Israel, The Book of Ezekiel, Chapter 19
s: The speaker is commanded to take up this lamentation, which is delivered through the images of the lioness and her cubs and of the vine. The chapter closes by stating that it is a lamentation and shall be for a lamentation.

l: The Book of Ezekiel, The Book of Ezekiel, Chapter 20
s: In the seventh year, elders of Israel come to inquire of the LORD, but he refuses to be inquired of by them and tells the son of man to judge them by recounting the abominations of their fathers. The LORD recalls choosing Israel in Egypt, bringing them out, and giving statutes, ordinances and Sabbaths, yet Israel repeatedly rebelled in Egypt and the wilderness, and the LORD acted for his name's sake, withheld full destruction, and swore to scatter them. The people continue the idolatry of their fathers, including sacrificing at high places and passing sons through the fire. The LORD declares he will be king over them with a mighty hand, gather them from the nations, judge them face to face in the wilderness of the peoples, purge rebels, and finally accept the faithful on his holy mountain and bring them into the land. The chapter ends with a prophecy against the forest of the south, where the LORD will kindle an unquenchable fire, and the prophet laments that people call him a speaker of parables.

l: the LORD, The Book of Ezekiel, Chapter 20
s: The LORD refuses to be inquired of by the elders and recounts how he chose Israel, rescued them, gave statutes and Sabbaths, and acted repeatedly for his name's sake despite their rebellion. He vows to rule over them with a mighty hand, gather them, judge and purge them, and accept them in the land so that they know he is the LORD. He also announces an unquenchable fire against the southern forest.

l: elders of Israel, The Book of Ezekiel, Chapter 20
s: Some elders of Israel come and sit before the prophet to inquire of the LORD in the seventh year, fifth month, tenth day. The LORD rejects their inquiry, swearing he will not be inquired of by them.

l: Israel, The Book of Ezekiel, Chapter 20
s: Israel is shown as a people chosen by the LORD who rebelled in Egypt and the wilderness, profaned his Sabbaths, and continued in idolatry, including child sacrifice, to the present day. The LORD promises to gather them, judge them, purge the rebels, and bring the rest into the land to serve him on his holy mountain, where they will loathe their past evils.

l: Ezekiel, The Book of Ezekiel, Chapter 20
s: The son of man is commanded to speak to the elders, judge them by making known their fathers' abominations, and prophesy to the house of Israel. He is also told to set his face toward the south and prophesy against its forest. At the end he cries "Ah Lord GOD!" because people say he is a speaker of parables.

l: fathers (of the children of Israel), The Book of Ezekiel, Chapter 20
s: The fathers rebelled in Egypt and the wilderness, rejected the LORD's ordinances, profaned his Sabbaths, and followed idols. The LORD swore they would not enter the land, spared them from full destruction, and later they blasphemed him by sacrificing at high hills and thick trees, giving rise to the name Bamah.

l: Egypt, The Book of Ezekiel, Chapter 20
s: Egypt is where the LORD made himself known to Israel and swore to bring them out to a good land. Israel did not forsake Egypt's idols there, and the LORD considered pouring out wrath in the middle of Egypt but acted for his name's sake and brought them out.

l: wilderness, The Book of Ezekiel, Chapter 20
s: The wilderness is where the LORD gave his statutes, ordinances and Sabbaths, and where Israel and then their children rebelled. There he swore not to bring that generation into the land and to scatter them later. He promises a future judgment "face to face" in the wilderness of the peoples, as he did with the fathers.

l: promised land (flowing with milk and honey), The Book of Ezekiel, Chapter 20
s: The land is described as one the LORD searched out, flowing with milk and honey, the glory of all lands. The rebellious wilderness generation was denied entry, and rebels purged in the future will not enter it. The LORD promises to bring the gathered Israel into it, the country sworn to their fathers.

l: idols, The Book of Ezekiel, Chapter 20
s: Idols, including the idols of Egypt and of the fathers, are what Israel refused to throw away and followed with their hearts and eyes. The LORD says Israel's gifts and sacrifices to them profane his name, and he tells them in irony to go serve them, though they will no longer profane his name.

l: statutes and ordinances, The Book of Ezekiel, Chapter 20
s: The LORD gave statutes and ordinances by which a man who does them will live, and Israel repeatedly rejected them. He also says he gave them statutes that were not good and ordinances in which they could not live, and polluted them in their gifts, in the passing of firstborn through the fire.

l: forest of the south, The Book of Ezekiel, Chapter 20
s: The forest of the south is the target of a prophecy: the LORD will kindle a fire in it that devours every green and dry tree. All faces from south to north will be burned.

l: fire (kindled in the southern forest), The Book of Ezekiel, Chapter 20
s: The LORD says he will kindle a fire that devours every green tree and every dry tree and will not be quenched. All flesh will see that the LORD has kindled it.

l: judgment of Israel, The Book of Ezekiel, Chapter 20
