s: The LORD will enter into judgment with Israel face to face in the wilderness of the peoples, as he did with their fathers. He will cause them to pass under the rod, bring them into the bond of the covenant, and purge out rebels, who will not enter the land of Israel.

l: gathering and return of Israel, The Book of Ezekiel, Chapter 20
s: The LORD promises to bring Israel out from the peoples and gather them from the countries where they are scattered, with a mighty hand and outstretched arm. He will bring them into the land, accept them on his holy mountain, and be sanctified in them before the nations. There they will remember and loathe their evil ways and know that he dealt with them for his name's sake.

l: The Book of Ezekiel, The Book of Ezekiel, Chapter 21
s: In Ezekiel 21 the LORD tells Ezekiel, addressed as son of man, to prophesy against Jerusalem and the land of Israel, announcing that he has drawn his sword to cut off the righteous and the wicked and that it will not return. Ezekiel is told to sigh with a broken heart, to cry out, and to strike his thigh and hands, because the coming news will make every heart melt. The sword is described as sharpened and polished for slaughter, set against the gates, and falling on the LORD's people and the princes of Israel. The king of Babylon stands at a fork in the road and uses divination, and the lot for Jerusalem decides his attack, though Ammon's Rabbah is also a possible target. The wounded wicked prince of Israel is told to remove his turban and crown, and the LORD says he will overturn the kingdom until the one whose right it is comes. Finally the LORD turns the sword against Ammon, promising judgment, wrath, and destruction by brutish men.

l: the LORD, The Book of Ezekiel, Chapter 21
s: The LORD declares that he is against Israel and has drawn his sword to cut off the righteous and the wicked, never to return it. He commands Ezekiel to prophesy, sigh, and mark out two ways for the Babylonian sword. He promises to overturn the crown of Israel until the one whose right it is comes, and to judge Ammon, pouring out his indignation and wrath on it.

l: Ezekiel, The Book of Ezekiel, Chapter 21
s: Ezekiel, addressed as son of man, receives several word-of-the-LORD commands in this unit. He is to set his face toward Jerusalem and prophesy against Israel, sigh bitterly before the people, cry and wail, and beat his thigh and strike his hands together. He is also to mark out two ways for the sword of the king of Babylon and to prophesy against the children of Ammon.

l: Israel, The Book of Ezekiel, Chapter 21
s: The land of Israel is told that the LORD is against it and that his sword will cut off the righteous and the wicked from the south to the north. His people and all the princes of Israel are delivered over to the sword. Its prince is called a deadly wounded wicked one whose day has come, and the kingdom is to be overturned until the rightful one comes.

l: Jerusalem, The Book of Ezekiel, Chapter 21
s: Jerusalem, called the fortified, is one of two destinations for the Babylonian sword. The king of Babylon's lot for Jerusalem points to battering rams against its gates, mounds, and forts. Its divination appears false to those who swore oaths to Babylon, but their iniquity is brought to memory so that they will be taken.

l: sword (the LORD's sword), The Book of Ezekiel, Chapter 21
s: The sword is drawn from its sheath, sharpened and polished to slaughter and flash like lightning, and given to the hand of the killer. It is set against all gates and is doubled to a third time as the sword of the fatally wounded great one. It will not return to its sheath for Israel, though the LORD later tells it to return in the case of Ammon. It is also identified with the sword of the king of Babylon coming along two ways.

l: king of Babylon, The Book of Ezekiel, Chapter 21
s: The king of Babylon stands at the parting of two ways and uses divination, shaking arrows, consulting the teraphim, and looking at the liver. His right-hand lot is for Jerusalem, where he is to set battering rams, cast up mounds, and build forts. His sword is to come by one of two ways, to Rabbah of Ammon or to Jerusalem.

l: children of Ammon, The Book of Ezekiel, Chapter 21
s: Ammon, whose city Rabbah is one target of the Babylonian sword, is the subject of a separate prophecy about its reproach. It is told that the sword is polished for slaughter while its people see false visions and divine lies. The LORD will judge it in the land of its birth, pour out his indignation, and deliver it to brutish men skillful to destroy. It will be fuel for the fire, its blood will be in the land, and it will be remembered no more.

l: prince of Israel, The Book of Ezekiel, Chapter 21
s: The prince of Israel is called a deadly wounded wicked one whose day has come in the time of the iniquity of the end. The LORD commands that his turban and crown be removed, that the low be exalted and the high humbled. His rule is to be overturned and will not be restored until the one whose right it is comes.

l: The Book of Ezekiel, The Book of Ezekiel, Chapter 22
s: In Ezekiel 22 the LORD commands the son of man to judge the bloody city and make known her abominations: bloodshed, idolatry, contempt for parents, oppression of foreigners, orphans and widows, sexual sins, bribery, usury, and profaning of the Sabbaths. He declares he will scatter the people among the nations to purge their filthiness. In a second word, the house of Israel is called dross in the furnace, and the LORD will gather them into Jerusalem to melt them with the fire of his wrath. In a third word, the land is described as uncleansed, with conspiring prophets, violent priests, wolf-like princes, and oppressive people of the land. The LORD sought a man to stand in the gap but found no one, so he poured out his indignation on them.

l: the LORD, The Book of Ezekiel, Chapter 22
s: The LORD speaks three words to the son of man, accusing the city and its leaders of bloodshed, idolatry, and oppression. He announces he will strike his hand at their dishonest gain, scatter them among the nations, and gather and melt them like dross in the furnace of his wrath. He sought someone to stand in the gap, found no one, and poured out his indignation on them.

l: Ezekiel, The Book of Ezekiel, Chapter 22
s: Addressed as son of man, Ezekiel receives the LORD's word three times. He is asked to judge the bloody city and make known her abominations, to hear that Israel has become dross, and to tell the land that it is not cleansed nor rained on in the day of indignation.

l: Jerusalem, The Book of Ezekiel, Chapter 22
s: Jerusalem is called the bloody city that sheds blood and makes idols that defile her. Her days are near their end and she becomes a reproach and mocking to the nations. The LORD will gather Israel into the middle of her as into a furnace to melt them in his wrath.

l: Israel, The Book of Ezekiel, Chapter 22
s: The house of Israel is called dross to the LORD, like bronze, tin, iron, and lead left over from silver. They will be gathered into Jerusalem and melted by the fire of his wrath, and will know that the LORD has poured out his wrath on them. They are also to be scattered among the nations.

l: princes of Israel, The Book of Ezekiel, Chapter 22
s: The princes of Israel are accused of shedding blood, each according to his power. They are likened to wolves ravening the prey, destroying souls to get dishonest gain.

l: prophets (Jerusalem's prophets), The Book of Ezekiel, Chapter 22
s: Jerusalem's prophets are accused of conspiracy, like a roaring lion devouring souls, taking treasure and making many widows. They plastered whitewash for the leaders with false visions and lies, saying 'The Lord GOD says' when the LORD had not spoken.

l: priests (Jerusalem's priests), The Book of Ezekiel, Chapter 22
s: The priests are charged with doing violence to the LORD's law and profaning his holy things. They made no distinction between holy and common or unclean and clean, and hid their eyes from his Sabbaths, so the LORD is profaned among them.

l: people of the land, The Book of Ezekiel, Chapter 22
s: The people of the land are accused of oppression and robbery. They troubled the poor and needy and wrongfully oppressed the foreigner.

l: furnace, The Book of Ezekiel, Chapter 22
s: The furnace serves as the image of judgment. As metals are gathered into its middle and melted by blown fire, so the LORD will gather Israel in Jerusalem and melt them in his anger and wrath.

l: dross, The Book of Ezekiel, Chapter 22
s: Dross is the LORD's description of the house of Israel, who are like bronze, tin, iron, and lead, the dross of silver. Because they have all become dross, they will be gathered and melted.

l: bloodshed, The Book of Ezekiel, Chapter 22
s: Bloodshed is the leading charge against the city, whose people shed blood within her, including through slander, bribes, and the princes' violence. It makes them guilty, and the LORD strikes his hand at the blood shed within her.

l: God's wrath, The Book of Ezekiel, Chapter 22
s: God's wrath is the fire the LORD will blow on Israel to melt them like metal in a furnace, so they will know he has poured it out. At the end, he says he has poured out his indignation, consumed them with the fire of his wrath, and brought their own way on their heads.

l: The Book of Ezekiel, The Book of Ezekiel, Chapter 23
s: The LORD gives Ezekiel an allegory of two sisters, Oholah (Samaria) and Oholibah (Jerusalem), who were unfaithful in Egypt in their youth and afterward. Oholah doted on the Assyrians and was handed over to them, who uncovered her nakedness, took her children, and killed her with the sword. Oholibah, more corrupt than her sister, lusted after the Assyrians and then the Babylonians (Chaldeans), and the LORD announces that these alienated lovers will attack her, strip her, and mutilate her, and that she will drink her sister's cup. The sisters are also charged with adultery with idols, shedding blood, sacrificing their sons to idols, and profaning the LORD's sanctuary and Sabbaths on the same day. The LORD says a mob will stone them, kill their children, and burn their houses so that lewdness ceases and they know he is the Lord GOD.

l: the LORD, The Book of Ezekiel, Chapter 23
s: The LORD speaks to Ezekiel, identifying the sisters as his own who bore him sons and daughters, and hands Oholah over to the Assyrians. He announces that he will raise up Oholibah's lovers against her, set his jealousy against her, and give her sister's cup into her hand. He charges both sisters with idolatry, child sacrifice, and profaning his sanctuary and Sabbaths, and promises that his judgment will end lewdness so that they know he is the Lord GOD.

l: Samaria, The Book of Ezekiel, Chapter 23
s: Oholah is the elder sister, representing Samaria, who played the prostitute in Egypt and again when she was the LORD's, doting on the Assyrians and defiling herself with their idols. The LORD delivered her into her lovers' hands; they uncovered her nakedness, took her sons and daughters, and killed her with the sword, making her a byword among women.

l: Jerusalem, The Book of Ezekiel, Chapter 23
s: Oholibah is the younger sister, representing Jerusalem, who saw her sister's fate yet became more corrupt, lusting after the Assyrians and then the Chaldeans she saw portrayed on a wall, to whom she sent messengers. The LORD becomes alienated from her, vows to bring her lovers against her, and says she will drink her sister's cup and bear her lewdness and prostitution.

l: Egypt, The Book of Ezekiel, Chapter 23
s: Egypt is where both sisters first played the prostitute in their youth, where their breasts were fondled. Oholibah later remembers those days and lusts after the Egyptians, and the LORD says he will make her stop remembering Egypt any more.

l: Assyrians, The Book of Ezekiel, Chapter 23
s: The Assyrians are the neighboring lovers, governors, rulers and horsemen, on whom Oholah doted and with whose idols she defiled herself. The LORD delivers Oholah into their hand, and they kill her and take her children; Oholibah also lusts after them, and they are named among the forces that will come against her.

l: Chaldea, The Book of Ezekiel, Chapter 23
s: The Babylonians (Chaldeans) are men portrayed on a wall in red whom Oholibah lusts after and sends messengers to, and who come to her bed and defile her. She becomes alienated from them, and the LORD promises to bring them with the Assyrians against her with weapons, chariots, and a company of peoples to judge her.

l: prostitution (spiritual unfaithfulness), The Book of Ezekiel, Chapter 23
s: Prostitution is the text's image for the sisters' unfaithfulness to the LORD, through foreign alliances, lovers, and idols, which began in Egypt and continued in Samaria and Jerusalem. The LORD declares he will make it cease so that all women may be taught not to be lewd, and that they will bear the sins of their idols.

l: idols, The Book of Ezekiel, Chapter 23
s: The sisters defile themselves with the idols of their lovers and commit adultery with them. They sacrifice the sons they bore to the LORD by making them pass through the fire to the idols, then enter the sanctuary the same day. Oholibah is told she will bear the sins of her idols.

l: cup of judgment (sister's cup), The Book of Ezekiel, Chapter 23
s: The cup is Oholah's (Samaria's) cup, deep, large, and full of drunkenness, sorrow, astonishment, desolation, ridicule, and derision. The LORD says he will give it into Oholibah's hand, and she will drink and drain it, gnaw its broken pieces, and tear her breasts.

l: judgment on Oholibah, The Book of Ezekiel, Chapter 23
s: The LORD will bring her alienated lovers, the Babylonians, Chaldeans, and Assyrians, against her on every side and commit the judgment to them. They will strip her clothes and jewels, take her labor, cut off her nose and ears, take her children, let her remnant fall by the sword, and burn the rest, and a mob will also stone her, so that she knows he is the Lord GOD.

l: The Book of Ezekiel, The Book of Ezekiel, Chapter 24
s: In the ninth year, the LORD tells Ezekiel to record the day the king of Babylon drew close to Jerusalem and to speak a parable to the rebellious house about a cauldron set on the fire, filled with choice pieces and bones and boiled until its rust is consumed. The cauldron stands for the bloody city, whose uncleansed filthiness and unhidden blood bring the LORD's unsparing judgment. The LORD then announces that he will take the desire of Ezekiel's eyes with one stroke and forbids him to mourn, and that evening Ezekiel's wife dies. When the people ask what this means, Ezekiel explains that the LORD will profane his sanctuary and their children will fall by the sword, and that they will likewise be unable to mourn but will pine away in their iniquities. The LORD says that Ezekiel will be a sign to them, and that when a survivor comes to report the news, Ezekiel's mouth will be opened and he will no longer be mute.

l: the LORD, The Book of Ezekiel, Chapter 24
s: The LORD gives Ezekiel the word about recording the day, the cauldron parable, and the command not to mourn his wife. He declares that he has spoken, will act, and will not go back, spare, or repent, and that he will profane his sanctuary and take the people's strength and children. He says the people will then know that he is the Lord GOD.

l: Ezekiel, The Book of Ezekiel, Chapter 24
s: Ezekiel is told to write down the day and to speak the cauldron parable to the rebellious house. He is told that the desire of his eyes will be taken and that he must not mourn aloud, weep, or eat mourner's bread, and he obeys after his wife dies in the evening. He explains the meaning to the people and is told he is a sign to them, and that his mouth will be opened to the survivor so he is no longer mute.

l: Jerusalem, The Book of Ezekiel, Chapter 24
s: Jerusalem is the city the king of Babylon drew close to on the very day the LORD spoke to Ezekiel. It is called the bloody city, the cauldron whose rust will not leave. Its sanctuary, which is the pride of its power, will be profaned, and its sons and daughters will fall by the sword.

l: rebellious house, The Book of Ezekiel, Chapter 24
s: The rebellious house is the audience of the cauldron parable that Ezekiel is told to utter. They ask what his behavior means, and he tells them they will do as he has done, unable to mourn and pining away in their iniquities. When this comes, they will know that the LORD is the Lord GOD.

l: cauldron (parable of the cauldron), The Book of Ezekiel, Chapter 24
s: The cauldron is set on the fire with water, filled with choice pieces such as the thigh and shoulder and choice bones, and boiled well with a great pile of wood. It is then set empty on the coals so its bronze burns and its filthiness and rust are melted and consumed. It represents the bloody city, whose great rust does not leave her and who will not be cleansed until the LORD's wrath rests.

l: Ezekiel's wife, The Book of Ezekiel, Chapter 24
s: Ezekiel's wife is the desire of his eyes, whom the LORD says he will take away with one stroke. She dies at evening, after Ezekiel had spoken to the people that morning. Ezekiel does not mourn her publicly, as commanded.

l: mourning customs, The Book of Ezekiel, Chapter 24
s: Ezekiel is forbidden to weep, make mourning for the dead, cover his lips, or eat mourner's bread, and must keep his headdress and sandals on. This conduct becomes a sign of what the people will do when the sanctuary is profaned and their children die. They will not mourn or weep but will pine away in their iniquities and moan to one another.

l: siege of Jerusalem, The Book of Ezekiel, Chapter 24
s: The text says the king of Babylon drew close to Jerusalem on the same day, in the ninth year, tenth month, tenth day, that the LORD's word came to Ezekiel. Ezekiel is told to write down that day. The cauldron parable portrays the coming fire and destruction of the city that follows.

l: The Book of Ezekiel, The Book of Ezekiel, Chapter 25
s: In Chapter 25 the LORD instructs the prophet, addressed as 'Son of man', to prophesy against four neighboring peoples who mocked or harmed Israel and Judah. The children of Ammon are condemned for saying 'Aha!' over the profaned sanctuary, the desolated land of Israel, and Judah's captivity, and will be handed to the children of the east and cut off. Moab and Seir are judged for saying Judah is like all the nations, and Moab's frontier cities will be opened to invaders. Edom is condemned for taking vengeance on Judah and will be made desolate from Teman to Dedan by the hand of Israel. The Philistines, who acted with perpetual hostility, will be cut off along with the Cherethites and the remnant of the sea coast, so that all will know that He is the LORD.

l: the LORD, The Book of Ezekiel, Chapter 25
s: The LORD speaks to the prophet and commands him to prophesy against Ammon, Moab, Edom, and the Philistines. He announces that he will stretch out his hand against them, delivering, cutting off, and destroying them. Repeatedly he states that the result will be that they know he is the LORD.

l: children of Ammon, The Book of Ezekiel, Chapter 25
s: The children of Ammon are accused of saying 'Aha!' against the sanctuary, the land of Israel, and the house of Judah, and of clapping, stamping, and rejoicing with contempt. They are to be delivered to the children of the east as a possession, with Rabbah made a stable for camels and Ammon a resting place for flocks. They will be plundered, cut off, and destroyed, and not remembered among the nations.

l: children of the east, The Book of Ezekiel, Chapter 25
s: The children of the east are to receive Ammon as a possession. They will set encampments and dwellings there, eat its fruit, and drink its milk. They will also be given access to Moab's frontier cities in order to go against Ammon.

l: Israel, The Book of Ezekiel, Chapter 25
s: The land of Israel is said to have been made desolate, and Ammon rejoiced over it with contempt. The LORD says he will lay his vengeance on Edom by the hand of his people Israel, who will act according to his anger and wrath.

l: Judah, The Book of Ezekiel, Chapter 25
s: The house of Judah is said to have gone into captivity, and Ammon mocked it. Moab and Seir claim that Judah is like all the nations, and Edom is accused of taking vengeance on Judah and greatly offending.

l: Moab, The Book of Ezekiel, Chapter 25
s: Moab, together with Seir, is accused of saying that the house of Judah is like all the nations. The LORD will open the side of Moab from its frontier cities, including Beth Jeshimoth, Baal Meon, and Kiriathaim, giving them to the children of the east. Judgments will be executed on Moab, and they will know that he is the LORD.

l: Edom, The Book of Ezekiel, Chapter 25
s: Edom is accused of dealing against Judah by taking vengeance and greatly offending. The LORD will cut off man and animal from it and make it desolate from Teman, with the people falling by the sword to Dedan. Israel will carry out his vengeance on Edom.

l: Philistines, The Book of Ezekiel, Chapter 25
s: The Philistines are accused of taking revenge and vengeance with contempt of soul, destroying with perpetual hostility. The LORD will stretch out his hand against them, cut off the Cherethites, and destroy the remnant of the sea coast. He will execute great vengeance with wrathful rebukes.

l: judgment and vengeance, The Book of Ezekiel, Chapter 25
s: Judgment takes the form of the LORD's announced punishments on each nation, each introduced by 'because' and 'therefore' and ending with the recognition that he is the LORD. Vengeance appears in two ways: Edom and the Philistines are condemned for taking vengeance, and the LORD in turn lays his own vengeance on them, with Edom's carried out by Israel.

l: The Book of Ezekiel, The Book of Ezekiel, Chapter 26
s: In the eleventh year, the LORD tells the prophet that because Tyre gloated over Jerusalem's fall, hoping to be replenished by it, the Lord GOD is against Tyre. He will bring many nations against it like waves, and specifically Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon with horses, chariots, and a large army from the north. The walls and towers will be broken, the people and its daughters in the field killed, its riches plundered, and its songs silenced, leaving a bare rock for spreading nets. The princes of the sea will mourn and tremble, and the islands will be dismayed at its fall. Tyre will be brought down to the pit with those of old, will never be inhabited or found again, while the Lord GOD sets glory in the land of the living.

l: Tyre, The Book of Ezekiel, Chapter 26
s: Tyre is condemned for saying 'Aha!' over Jerusalem's breaking and expecting to be replenished by her ruin. The Lord GOD declares he is against it: its walls and towers will fall, its wealth be plundered, its songs cease, and it will become a bare rock for spreading nets, brought down to the pit and never found again.

l: Jerusalem, The Book of Ezekiel, Chapter 26
s: Jerusalem is described by Tyre as broken and laid waste, the one who was the gateway of the peoples. Tyre expects to profit from her fall, which is the reason given for judgment against Tyre.

l: the LORD, The Book of Ezekiel, Chapter 26
s: The Lord GOD declares himself against Tyre and announces he will bring many nations and Nebuchadnezzar against it. He says he will make it a bare rock, cause its fall to shake the islands, bring it down to the pit, and set glory in the land of the living, so that they will know he is the LORD.

l: king of Babylon, The Book of Ezekiel, Chapter 26
s: Nebuchadnezzar, king of Babylon and king of kings, is to be brought by the Lord GOD against Tyre from the north with horses, chariots, horsemen, and a large army. He will kill its daughters in the field, build forts and a mound, break its walls and towers with battering engines and axes, and enter its gates.

l: many nations, The Book of Ezekiel, Chapter 26
s: Many nations will be caused to come up against Tyre as the sea causes its waves to rise. Tyre will become plunder for the nations.

l: destruction of Tyre, The Book of Ezekiel, Chapter 26
s: The destruction is described in detail: siege works, broken walls and towers, trampled streets, slain people, plundered riches, and stones, timber, and dust thrown into the waters. The islands and princes of the sea will tremble and lament, and Tyre will become a terror that is sought but never found again.

l: The Book of Ezekiel, The Book of Ezekiel, Chapter 27
s: The LORD instructs Ezekiel, addressed as son of man, to take up a lamentation over Tyre, the merchant city at the entry of the sea that boasted 'I am perfect in beauty.' The chapter pictures Tyre as a magnificent ship, built with cypress from Senir, a Lebanon cedar mast, Bashan oak oars, and Egyptian linen sails, and crewed by men of Sidon, Arvad, and Gebal. Tyre's army included Persia, Lud, Put, and Arvad, and its trade drew merchants from Tarshish, Javan, Judah, Israel, Damascus, Arabia, Sheba, and many other places, dealing in metals, horses, spices, wool, and precious stones. The ship is then broken by the east wind in the heart of the seas, and all its wealth, crew, and company sink in the day of its ruin. Mariners and pilots mourn on the shore with dust, ashes, shaved heads, and sackcloth, while island inhabitants and kings are horrified and the merchants hiss at Tyre's terrible end.

l: Tyre, The Book of Ezekiel, Chapter 27
s: Tyre is addressed as the merchant of the peoples to many islands who dwells at the entry of the sea and claims to be perfect in beauty. It is portrayed as a richly built, well-staffed, wealthy trading city that enriched the kings of the earth. It is broken by the seas, brought to silence, and will be no more.

l: the LORD, The Book of Ezekiel, Chapter 27
s: The LORD's word comes again to Ezekiel, instructing him to take up a lamentation over Tyre. As the Lord GOD, he is the speaker of the message that recounts Tyre's boasted beauty and its coming ruin.
